description: A group of motivated people interested in creating a creative and unique project.
summary:
We built Lumen, an interactive lunar mission planner that helps users explore where and when a mission could operate on the Moon. It uses NASA terrain data and JPL orbital data to compare locations based on sunlight, Earth visibility, terrain, and mission priorities. Users can explore the Moon in 3D, compare sites side by side, and see how changing mission dates affects solar power, battery reserves, and opportunities to communicate with Earth.

Lumen addresses the CLPS Lunar Mission Browser challenge by bringing complex datasets into one visual planning tool. Near the lunar south pole, a nearby ridge can block sunlight or Earth, and a launch delay can change a site’s operating window. These details matter when a mission depends on limited power and communication opportunities. Lumen makes those tradeoffs easier to understand, helping students, educators, and early mission planners explore their options and see the evidence behind each comparison.
details:
Lumen lets users explore the Moon in 3D, rank candidate sites, and compare how different locations and mission dates affect sunlight, Earth visibility, solar power, and battery reserves. Users can also test how a launch delay changes their options.

We built it with Python and TypeScript, using NASA terrain data, JPL orbital data, and OpenVINO for an optional local AI assistant. The creative part is bringing terrain, timing, and mission priorities into one interactive workspace where users can see why the results change.

Our goal is to make early lunar mission planning more accessible to students, educators, and planners. We focused on scientific accuracy, ease of use, accessibility, and performance, while making the data sources and assumptions clear.
